dom.t: Career inequality: Professional change preserves unequal rewards

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source does not assess AI’s jagged task-level capabilities, verification needs or selective deployment directly. It instead reframes work redesign as a longer-term institutional question: disruption may be absorbed without changing legal hierarchies, while lawyers’ professional conservatism can both preserve public values and impede innovation.
qs: Because many of the things that come along as disruptions can be absorbed into existing hierarchies without changing them.

But when lawyers turn that lens on their own professional institutions and values, it can lead to a kind of inertia and resistance to doing anything new, because it’s not the way we’ve always done it.

st.t: Career inequality: Professional change preserves unequal rewards
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition: longitudinal evidence shows that elite educational credentials, race and gender continue to shape prestigious and highly rewarded career outcomes despite substantial professional change and diversity efforts. It also supports the cluster’s qualifications that these are average rather than deterministic patterns, career satisfaction can coexist with unequal rewards, and future disruption may be absorbed by existing hierarchies.
qs: But on the contrary, the benefits of going to a top-ranked law school actually increase over the course of a lawyer’s career in terms of income, opportunities for prestigious jobs, and the ability to repay law school debt, according to the findings of a 20-year longitudinal study of the careers of lawyers.
Because many of the things that come along as disruptions can be absorbed into existing hierarchies without changing them.

st.t: Lawyer development: AI renews lifelong competence reform
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s account of institutional barriers to competence reform: it argues that technological disruption can be absorbed without changing professional hierarchies and that lawyers’ conservatism can produce inertia within their own institutions. It adds caution rather than a competing reform model, and calls for long-term research instead of claiming measured career effects.

kp.k: Longitudinal evidence tracks careers and inequality across two decades
kp.d: The article reports on “After the JD,” a quantitative and qualitative study of more than 5,000 law graduates who entered the bar in 2000, drawn from nearly every US law school, including unaccredited schools. Surveys occurred in 2002-2003, 2007, and 2012-2013; 2,035 respondents completed all three, with career tracking through 2019 and additional interviews. Conducted in partnership with the National Association for Law Placement and the American Bar Foundation, its conclusions appeared in a 2023 book. This is evidence about legal careers and institutional continuity, not a study of AI adoption or effects.
qs: This and many other myth-busting conclusions are the result of “After the JD,” a quantitative and qualitative analysis that includes more than 5,000 law graduates who entered the bar in 2000.

These graduates were surveyed three times over the course of the project — in 2002-2003, 2007, and 2012-2013, with career tracking through LinkedIn and other sources through 2019 — with 2,035 respondents answering all three surveys.

kp.k: Elite law school advantages increase rather than fade
kp.d: McArdle reports that the study contradicts the assumption that academic credentials lose importance as demonstrated work quality becomes more important. Attendance at a top-ranked law school was associated with increasing career advantages in income, prestigious employment opportunities, and capacity to repay law school debt.
qs: But on the contrary, the benefits of going to a top-ranked law school actually increase over the course of a lawyer’s career in terms of income, opportunities for prestigious jobs, and the ability to repay law school debt, according to the findings of a 20-year longitudinal study of the careers of lawyers.

kp.k: Career hierarchies persist despite substantial professional change
kp.d: David Wilkins interprets the study as showing remarkable continuity in career structures and access to prestigious, highly paid positions. He identifies white men with children as the group doing best on average at both the beginning and end of the study, explicitly qualifying this as a group-level finding rather than a universal description of individual outcomes.
qs: While there have been some tremendous changes, there is also remarkable continuity when we look at many of the structures beneath the surface of how the bar and the legal profession are organized, how careers operate, and who tends to end up in the most prestigious, high-paying positions.
The people who are doing the best are white men with children.
That doesn’t mean every white man with children succeeds — or that every woman or person of color doesn’t — but on average [that’s what the study found].

kp.k: Firm practices reproduce inequality despite diversity investment
kp.d: Explaining the book’s argument about racialization, Wilkins says hiring, development, promotion, and firm culture reproduce assumptions about the right kind of lawyer and reinforce inequality even without intentional discrimination. He acknowledges racism but does not regard it as the main explanation for disappointing progress. Against firms’ spending of tens of millions of dollars, probably collectively more, on diversity, he estimates Black lawyers remain maybe 3% of partners and an even smaller share of powerful equity partners; these are his approximate figures, not a separately specified statistical result.
qs: There’s a chapter in the book about how the ways in which law firms hire, develop, and promote people, and the culture of law firms, still today reinforce a view of who the right kind of lawyer is — what the fit of that lawyer is, what that lawyer looks like, and where that lawyer comes from.
And that reinforces the inequalities of that process, even in the absence of intentional discrimination.
Firms have spent tens of millions of dollars, probably collectively even more, promoting diversity.
Black lawyers still constitute maybe 3% of the partners.
And if you look at the equity partners that have power in these organizations, it would be an even smaller percentage.

kp.k: Career satisfaction extends beyond elite large-firm success
kp.d: The article reports that lawyers are generally satisfied with their careers, contrary to widespread perceptions. Wilkins describes qualitative accounts of solo and small-firm practitioners who value autonomy, control, and helping clients while earning a good living. He qualifies the comparison with major-firm partnership: earnings are lower on average than that hypothetical outcome, while greater happiness is at least the practitioners’ own perception.
qs: The result is a trove of data on everything from whether lawyers are satisfied in their careers — they generally are, despite widespread perceptions that they are unhappy — to how factors including gender, race, socioeconomic class, and law school status affect their professional development.
We tell the stories of solo and small-firm practitioners who are extremely happy and successful at what they do.
They feel like they have control and autonomy over their practices; they feel like they’re really helping their clients.

And they’re making a good living — not on average what they might have made if they had one day become a partner in a major law firm, but they’re much happier, or at least, they think of themselves as much happier.

kp.k: Disruptions can be absorbed into existing professional hierarchies
kp.d: Asked about the next 20 years, Wilkins cautions against assuming that anticipated changes will fundamentally reshape the bar’s social structure or legal career organization. His proposed mechanism is that established hierarchies can absorb disruptions without changing. This is a forward-looking caution informed by historical findings, not an AI-specific prediction or evidence of AI’s effects.
qs: But what the book should make us cautious about is expecting that these changes will fundamentally alter the social structure of the bar or the big structural aspects of how law and careers in the legal profession work in this country.
Because many of the things that come along as disruptions can be absorbed into existing hierarchies without changing them.

kp.k: Professional conservatism protects institutions but can impede internal reform
kp.d: Wilkins identifies globalization, technology, and sophisticated consumers’ growing power over producers as pressures for change. He argues that lawyers’ habit of questioning change can help preserve democracy, the rule of law, and liberty, while acknowledging that lawyers also sometimes undermine those values. Applied to their own professional institutions, the same habit can produce inertia. He hopes future researchers will examine how these competing forces shape careers over the next 20 years.
qs: As much as things are changing with globalization, technology, the rise of sophisticated consumers exercising power over producers, if the last few years have taught us anything, it’s that there are a lot of things that should not change, like democracy, rule of law, individual freedom, and liberty.
One factor that underlies both the positive and the negative roles that lawyers play in society is that “thinking like a lawyer” often means raising challenges or questions about change.

But when lawyers turn that lens on their own professional institutions and values, it can lead to a kind of inertia and resistance to doing anything new, because it’s not the way we’ve always done it.
I’m hoping that a young and energetic team of socio-legal researchers will decide to study how the interplay of these forces shape lawyers’ careers over the next 20 years!

kp.k: Career evidence should inform students, curricula, and public understanding
kp.d: Wilkins says the authors intend the findings to help law students consider career goals, law schools design curricula, and the public understand access to the profession and its opportunity structures. This is a statement of intended uses for the research, not evidence that curricula or career choices have already changed.
qs: Wilkins says the authors hope the abundance of “rich data” the book offers will be useful to three groups in particular: law students as they consider what they want from their careers; law schools as they design curricula to best serve students; and the public

What the profession looks like, who has access to it, and what the structures of opportunity are, are matters of interest and importance and concern far beyond the legal profession to our society as a whole.
